title: Sukūn & hamza + reading words with ع and ح
objectives: Student can read a letter carrying a sukūn as a closed syllable — no vowel added after it, no lengthening — and can name the five qalqalah letters (ق ط ب ج د) and bounce them.
Student can recognise the hamza in all five of its seats (أ إ ؤ ئ ء), produce it as a clean glottal stop, and keep it distinct from ع in minimal pairs such as عَمَل / أَمَل.

Student can read roughly 40 fully-vocalised real words containing ع or ح, in initial, medial and final position, holding the correct makhraj — including the hardest case, a bare ع or ح at the end of a word.
Student can state the beginner-level difference between hamzat al-qaṭʿ (always pronounced) and hamzat al-waṣl (skipped when joined), using الـ as the worked example.

slides.heading: Lesson 1.13 — Sukūn & hamza, then ع and ح inside words
What changes today
body: Until now every letter you read carried a vowel — fatha, kasra or damma. Today two new marks join them, and then you stop reading single letters and start reading WORDS.
A sukūn ( ْ ) means the opposite of a vowel: this letter has none. Close it and stop.
A hamza ( ء ) is a sound you have been making your whole life without knowing its name — the catch in the middle of ‘uh-oh’.
Everything after that is real words, chosen so that the two letters you find hardest — ع and ح — come back again and again.

slides.heading: Sukūn — the letter with no vowel
body: A fatha, kasra or damma OPENS a letter into a vowel: بَ is ‘ba’, بِ is ‘bi’, بُ is ‘bu’.
A sukūn CLOSES it: بْ is just ‘b’, with nothing after it.
Two letters joined this way make one syllable you say in a single beat — بَعْ is ‘baʿ’, not ‘ba-ʿa’.
The mistake to avoid: adding a little vowel after the closed letter. ‘baʿ-uh’ is wrong. Stop the sound dead.
The other mistake: stretching it. A sukūn never lengthens a letter — that is a different mark you will meet in Phase 3.

slides.heading: Sukūn on the hard letters
slides.instructions: Each unit is two letters: the first carries a fatha, the second carries a sukūn. A sukūn means NO vowel — close the letter and stop. Read across, right to left.

audio.cue: بَعْ: ba, then ع closed by a sukūn. The ع has no vowel — squeeze the middle of the throat shut and stop there. Do not add an ‘uh’ after it.
بَحْ: ba, then ح closed by a sukūn — a bare breath from the middle of the throat, cut off clean. No vowel after it.
بَصْ: ba, then ص closed by a sukūn. Hold the whistle a moment with the tongue-body raised, then stop. The fatha before it darkens: closer to ‘bo’ than ‘ba’.
بَضْ: ba, then ض closed by a sukūn. Press the SIDE of the tongue against the upper molars and hold — this is where ض is made, not the tongue-tip.
بَطْ: ba, then ط closed by a sukūn. ط is a qalqalah letter — it must BOUNCE: a dry echo, ‘baT-eh’, with no real vowel added.
بَظْ: ba, then ظ closed by a sukūn. ظ is NOT a qalqalah letter — do not bounce it. Tongue-tip between the teeth, voiced and heavy, and let it die away.
تَعْ: ta, then ع closed by a sukūn. Same closed ع as بَعْ, now after a light letter — the contrast makes the ع easier to hear.
سَحْ: sa, then ح closed by a sukūn. س is a sharp hiss at the front, ح is deep breath at the throat — jump straight from one to the other.
مَصْ: ma, then ص closed by a sukūn. Lips, then the heavy whistle. Keep the tongue-body domed all the way to the stop.
نَطْ: na, then ط closed by a sukūn — bounce it, ‘naT-eh’.

slides.heading: Five letters that bounce — a first look at qalqalah
body: Five letters cannot be stopped silently, because your voice-box is closed while you make them: ق ط ب ج د, remembered as قطب جد.
When one of them carries a sukūn, releasing it makes a small dry echo. That echo is called qalqalah.
Say مَدْ. You cannot end it without a faint ‘-eh’ escaping. That is qalqalah, and it is correct.
For now, one rule only: these five bounce, and nothing else does. ط is the one that matters most to you, because it is also a heavy letter.
The full rules — how strong the bounce is in each position — are a Phase 3 topic. Do not chase them yet.

slides.heading: The five bouncing letters — قطب جد
slides.instructions: These five letters (ق ط ب ج د) bounce when they carry a sukūn. Say each one and listen for a small dry echo — never a real vowel.

audio.cue: مَقْ: ق carries a sukūn, so it bounces — ‘maq-eh’. ق is one of the five qalqalah letters.
مَطْ: ط carries a sukūn, so it bounces — ‘maT-eh’, heavy and dry.
مَبْ: ب carries a sukūn, so it bounces — the lips part with a small echo.
مَجْ: ج carries a sukūn, so it bounces — ‘maj-eh’.
مَدْ: د carries a sukūn, so it bounces — ‘mad-eh’.

slides.heading: Bounce or hold? — ط vs ظ, د vs ذ
slides.instructions: Alternate down the row. Two of these bounce and two do not. If ظ bounces, you have swapped it for a heavy د.

audio.cue: مَطْ: ط bounces. Dry echo, no vowel added.
مَظْ: ظ does NOT bounce. Tongue-tip between the teeth, voiced, heavy — hold it and let it fade.
مَدْ: د bounces — it is one of the five قطب جد letters.
مَذْ: ذ does NOT bounce. Same tongue position as ظ but light, not heavy.
ء: a clean glottal stop — the catch in the middle of ‘uh-oh’, or the little break before each word in ‘apple, apple, apple’. It comes from the very bottom of the throat, at the vocal cords.

slides.makhraj: the vocal cords, at the very bottom of the throat (aqṣā al-ḥalq)
notes: You already make this sound constantly in your own speech — the task is not to learn it, but to notice it and write it.
It is the deepest of all the throat sounds. ء is at the bottom, ح is in the middle, and ع is in the middle too but VOICED — that is why ع and ء get confused.
Unlike the other 28 letters, hamza has no fixed shape of its own. It rides on a seat — أ إ ؤ ئ — or sits bare on the line: ء.

slides.heading: The seats of the hamza
body: The hamza sound never changes. Only the chair it sits on changes, and the chair is chosen by the vowels around it.
أ — on an alif. The commonest seat, used at the start of almost every word: أَحَد, أَمَل.
إ — under an alif. Always means the hamza carries a kasra: إِيمَان.
ؤ — on a waaw. The waaw is only furniture; you do not say ‘w’: مُؤْمِن.
ئ — on a yaa, which loses its dots. You do not say ‘y’: بِئْر.
ء — no seat at all, sitting on the line, usually at the end of a word: ضَوْء, شَيْء.
You do not need to predict which seat a word uses. You need to recognise all five and read them as one sound.

slides.heading: Two kinds of hamza: one you always say, one you often skip
body: Hamzat al-qaṭʿ (أ) is the ordinary one. You pronounce it every single time, wherever it falls: أَحَد, أَمَل, سَأَل.
Hamzat al-waṣl (ٱ) is a starter hamza. Think of it as a door, not a sound: if you START there you walk through it and it sounds. If you are already walking, it is not there.
You have said this thousands of times already. اِسْم on its own is ‘ism’. But بِسْمِ ٱللَّٰه is ‘bismillāh’ — not ‘bi-ismillāh’. The alif of اِسْم vanished.
The same happens with الـ ‘the’. Alone you say al-ḥamdu. Joined, in بِٱلصَّبْرِ, you say bi-ṣ-ṣabr.
The test: put وَ in front and read it joined. If the hamza disappears it is waṣl (وَٱسْم → wasm). If it survives it is qaṭʿ (وَأَخ → wa-ʾakh).
Beginner rule, and it is enough for now: if the alif has a hamza drawn on or under it (أ إ), say it every time. If it is bare and something comes before it, slide past.

slides.heading: Hamza in every seat
slides.instructions: The hamza is always the same sound — a clean catch in the throat. Only its SEAT changes: أ إ ؤ ئ, or no seat at all. Name the seat, then read the word.

audio.cue: Read أَحَد right to left: hamza on alif + fatha (a), ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), dal (d), then blend: aḥad — “one”. The hamza is a clean catch in the throat — the sound in the middle of ‘uh-oh’.
Read أَمَل right to left: hamza on alif + fatha (a), meem + fatha (ma), lam (l), then blend: amal — “hope”. Compare it in a moment with عَمَل — same word shape, different first sound.
Read إِيمَان right to left: hamza UNDER the alif + kasra (i), yaa as a long ī, meem + fatha (mā), nun (n), then blend: īmān — “faith”. A hamza written under the alif always carries a kasra.
Read سَأَل right to left: seen + fatha (sa), hamza on alif + fatha (ʾa), lam (l), then blend: saʾal — “he asked”. The hamza sits in the middle here — the word breaks cleanly in two.

Read رَأْس right to left: ra + fatha (ra), hamza on alif with SUKŪN (a clean catch, no vowel), seen (s), then blend: raʾs — “head”. Sukūn and hamza together — stop the throat, then release into the seen.

Read مُؤْمِن right to left: meem + damma (mu), hamza on waaw with sukūn (ʾ), meem + kasra (mi), nun (n), then blend: muʾmin — “believer”. When the hamza rides a waaw it is written ؤ — the waaw is only a seat, it is not pronounced ‘w’.
Read بِئْر right to left: ba + kasra (bi), hamza on yaa with sukūn (ʾ), ra (r), then blend: biʾr — “a well”. When the hamza rides a yaa it is written ئ and the yaa loses its dots.

Read ضَوْء right to left: ḍaad + fatha (ḍaw, heavy), waaw with sukūn, hamza ALONE on the line (ʾ), then blend: ḍawʾ — “light”. At the end of a word after a sukūn the hamza sits on the line with no seat at all.
Read شَيْء right to left: sheen + fatha (sha), yaa with sukūn (y), hamza alone on the line (ʾ), then blend: shayʾ — “a thing”. Same seatless hamza as ضَوْء. Very common — you will meet it constantly.

Read قَرَأَ right to left: qaaf + fatha (qa), ra + fatha (ra), hamza on alif + fatha (ʾa), then blend: qaraʾa — “he read”. Lesson 1.12 promised this word would come back — here is the hamza it was hiding.

slides.heading: ع is not ء — the difference that changes meaning
body: This is the single most common substitution beginners make, and it is not a small one: عَمَل is ‘a deed’, أَمَل is ‘hope’.
ء comes from the very bottom of the throat, at the vocal cords. Nothing squeezes; the sound simply stops and starts.
ع comes from the MIDDLE of the throat, and it is voiced. The throat narrows and you feel a squeeze that you can hold: ʿaaaa.
Test one — stretch it. You can hold a ع for three seconds. You cannot hold a ء at all; it is a catch, not a sound.
Test two — put a finger on your throat, on the Adam’s apple. On ع you feel a buzz the whole way through. On ء you feel one click and then nothing. Let your finger tell you, not your ear.

slides.heading: ع or ء? — read down each column
slides.instructions: Each pair differs by one letter only. ع is squeezed in the middle of the throat and voiced; ء is a clean catch at the top. Read the pair back to back until they sound different.

audio.cue: Read عَمَل right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), meem + fatha (ma), lam (l), then blend: ʿamal — “deed, work”. ʿayn: squeeze the MIDDLE of the throat and voice it.
Read أَمَل right to left: hamza + fatha (a), meem + fatha (ma), lam (l), then blend: amal — “hope”. hamza: a clean catch at the very TOP of the throat. Nothing squeezes.
Read عَلَم right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), lam + fatha (la), meem (m), then blend: ʿalam — “flag, sign”.
Read أَلَم right to left: hamza + fatha (a), lam + fatha (la), meem (m), then blend: alam — “pain”.
Read عَرْض right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ra with sukūn (r), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: ʿarḍ — “width”.
Read أَرْض right to left: hamza + fatha (a), ra with sukūn (r), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: arḍ — “earth, land”. Both words end in ض — the FIRST letter is the only difference.
ع: middle of the throat, voiced and squeezed. Say ‘aa’ and slowly tighten the middle of your throat until the sound thickens — that thickening is the ع.

slides.makhraj: the middle of the throat (wasaṭ al-ḥalq)
notes: Revision letter — you met ع in Lesson 1.5. Today it is back inside whole words, which is much harder than saying it alone.
Test yourself with a hand on your throat: ع buzzes, ح does not. Same place, one voiced, one not.
The position that catches everyone is ع at the END of a word, with no vowel after it to lean on — سَمْع, دَمْع. Sustain it for a beat.

slides.heading: ع inside real words — start, middle, end
slides.instructions: Read right to left. The ع gets harder as it moves toward the end of the word — the last row has nothing after the ع to lean on.

audio.cue: Read عَبْد right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ba with sukūn (b), dal (d), then blend: ʿabd — “servant”. The sukūn on ب gives you time to hold the ع open first.
Read عَسَل right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), seen + fatha (sa), lam (l), then blend: ʿasal — “honey”.
Read عَيْن right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), yaa with sukūn (y), nun (n), then blend: ʿayn — “eye; spring”. This is the letter’s own name — if you can say the word, you can say the letter.

Read عِلْم right to left: ʿayn + kasra (ʿi), lam with sukūn (l), meem (m), then blend: ʿilm — “knowledge”. ʿayn with a kasra is the hardest start of all — the throat wants to relax into a plain hamza.
Read عَصْر right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ṣaad with sukūn (ṣ, heavy), ra (r), then blend: ʿaṣr — “afternoon, time”. Two back sounds in a row. The ص darkens the fatha before it.
Read بَعْد right to left: ba + fatha (ba), ʿayn with sukūn (ʿ), dal (d), then blend: baʿd — “after”. A sukūn’d ع mid-word gets squeezed — that squeeze is exactly the muscle to train.
Read بَعْض right to left: ba + fatha (ba), ʿayn with sukūn (ʿ), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: baʿḍ — “some”.
Read جَعَلَ right to left: jeem + fatha (ja), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), lam + fatha (la), then blend: jaʿala — “he made”. Keep the ع voiced right through the middle — do not let it become a silent stop.
Read نَعَمْ right to left: nun + fatha (na), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), meem with sukūn (m), then blend: naʿam — “yes”. A word you can actually use out loud today.
Read مَعَ right to left: meem + fatha (ma), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), then blend: maʿa — “with”. Two letters — the easiest ع in the language. Start here if the others fight you.

Read سَمِعَ right to left: seen + fatha (sa), meem + kasra (mi), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), then blend: samiʿa — “he heard”. The vowel after the ع gives you somewhere to land — the easiest of the final group.
Read رَفَعَ right to left: ra + fatha (ra), fa + fatha (fa), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), then blend: rafaʿa — “he raised”.
Read رَجَعَ right to left: ra + fatha (ra), jeem + fatha (ja), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), then blend: rajaʿa — “he returned”.

Read سَمْع right to left: seen + fatha (sa), meem with sukūn (m), ʿayn with sukūn (ʿ), then blend: samʿ — “hearing”. A bare ع at the very end with nothing after it — the hardest shape there is. Sustain it for a beat; do not drop it.
Read دَمْع right to left: dal + fatha (da), meem with sukūn (m), ʿayn with sukūn (ʿ), then blend: damʿ — “tears”. Same shape as سَمْع. Drill the two as a rhyming pair.
ح: middle of the throat, unvoiced — a warm breath, as if fogging a cold window, but tighter and from lower down. No buzz at all.

slides.makhraj: the middle of the throat (wasaṭ al-ḥalq)
notes: Revision letter — you met ح in Lesson 1.2. Today it is back inside whole words.
ح is the unvoiced twin of ع: identical place in the throat, but no voice. ه is a softer, looser breath from higher up, and خ scrapes at the back of the mouth.
The diagnostic: if حَمْد, بَحْر and صُبْح are all correct, you own the letter. If only حَمْد is right, you are copying it at the start of a word and defaulting to ه everywhere else.

slides.heading: ح inside real words
slides.instructions: Read right to left. Keep a hand on your throat: ح should feel tight in the middle, with no voice buzzing.

audio.cue: Read حَمْد right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), meem with sukūn (m), dal (d), then blend: ḥamd — “praise”. You hear this every day in al-Fātiḥah — anchor the ح sound here first.
Read حَقّ right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), qaaf with a shadda (qq — held double), then blend: ḥaqq — “truth”. Two throat sounds back to back. Keep ق deep and ح breathy; they are not the same place.
Read حَبْل right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), ba with sukūn (b), lam (l), then blend: ḥabl — “rope”.
Read حَجَر right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), jeem + fatha (ja), ra (r), then blend: ḥajar — “stone”.
Read حُبّ right to left: ḥaa + damma (ḥu), ba with a shadda (bb — held double), then blend: ḥubb — “love”. The damma rounds your lips — do not let the ح slide into a plain English ‘h’.
Read بَحْر right to left: ba + fatha (ba), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), ra (r), then blend: baḥr — “sea”. A sukūn’d ح is pure friction with no vowel to hide behind.
Read لَحْم right to left: lam + fatha (la), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), meem (m), then blend: laḥm — “meat”. Squeezed between two easy letters — listen for the ح vanishing entirely.
Read تَحْتَ right to left: ta + fatha (ta), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), ta + fatha (ta), then blend: taḥta — “under”.
Read سِحْر right to left: seen + kasra (si), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), ra (r), then blend: siḥr — “magic”. A sharp front hiss, then a deep throat breath — a big jump, made fast.
Read صُبْح right to left: ṣaad + damma (ṣu, heavy), ba with sukūn (b), ḥaa (ḥ), then blend: ṣubḥ — “morning”. A final ح is the one most often dropped. Finish the breath so it is audible.

slides.heading: ح or خ or ه? — read down each column
slides.instructions: Each pair differs by one letter only. These are real, different words — the sound change changes the meaning.

audio.cue: Read حَلَقَ right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), lam + fatha (la), qaaf + fatha (qa), then blend: ḥalaqa — “he shaved”. The most consequential pair in the Qurʾān: get the ح wrong here and ‘He created’ becomes ‘he shaved’.

Read خَلَقَ right to left: khaa + fatha (kha), lam + fatha (la), qaaf + fatha (qa), then blend: khalaqa — “he created”. خ scrapes at the back of the mouth; ح is a clean breath lower down in the throat.
Read نَحْل right to left: nun + fatha (na), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), lam (l), then blend: naḥl — “bees”.
Read نَخْل right to left: nun + fatha (na), khaa with sukūn (kh), lam (l), then blend: nakhl — “date palms”.
Read فَحْم right to left: fa + fatha (fa), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), meem (m), then blend: faḥm — “charcoal”.

Read فَهْم right to left: fa + fatha (fa), haa with sukūn (h), meem (m), then blend: fahm — “understanding”. ه is a soft breath from the very top of the throat; ح squeezes in the middle. Hand on the throat: ح is tight, ه is loose.

slides.heading: Hear a reciter say it — real Qurʾanic words
slides.instructions: These are the exact words as they appear in the Qurʾān, tanwīn and all. Tap each one to hear a qāriʾ say it, then copy him out loud.

audio.cue: A sukūn closes the letter. No vowel after it, and no stretching.

items.name: qalqalah — ق ط ب ج د bounce

audio.cue: The five letters قطب جد bounce when they carry a sukūn. A dry echo, never a real vowel.

items.name: hamza — a catch in the throat

audio.cue: One sound, five seats: أ إ ؤ ئ ء.
Squeezed and buzzing. You can hold it for three seconds.
Same place as ع, but no buzz at all.

slides.heading: Homework — 15–20 min/day
tasks: Read the sukūn ladder aloud once (بَعْ بَحْ بَصْ بَضْ بَطْ / بَظْ تَعْ سَحْ مَصْ نَطْ), stopping each second letter dead — no added vowel
Bounce-or-hold drill, 3 times through: مَطْ (bounce) — مَظْ (hold) — مَدْ (bounce) — مَذْ (hold)
Write the ten hamza words in your notebook, and next to each one write which seat it uses (أ إ ؤ ئ or none)
Read the ع word set aloud daily, all three rows — start, middle and end. Say the last row (سَمْع دَمْع) twice as often as the rest
Read the ح word set aloud daily, then the ح/خ/ه pairs across, never down
Tap through the seven reciter words and copy him out loud, once per day

Read سَأَل right to left: seen + fatha (sa), hamza on alif + fatha (ʾa), lam (l), then blend: saʾal — “he asked”. The hamza sits in the middle here — the word breaks cleanly in two.

Read رَأْس right to left: ra + fatha (ra), hamza on alif with SUKŪN (a clean catch, no vowel), seen (s), then blend: raʾs — “head”. Sukūn and hamza together — stop the throat, then release into the seen.

Read مُؤْمِن right to left: meem + damma (mu), hamza on waaw with sukūn (ʾ), meem + kasra (mi), nun (n), then blend: muʾmin — “believer”. When the hamza rides a waaw it is written ؤ — the waaw is only a seat, it is not pronounced ‘w’.
Read بِئْر right to left: ba + kasra (bi), hamza on yaa with sukūn (ʾ), ra (r), then blend: biʾr — “a well”. When the hamza rides a yaa it is written ئ and the yaa loses its dots.

Read ضَوْء right to left: ḍaad + fatha (ḍaw, heavy), waaw with sukūn, hamza ALONE on the line (ʾ), then blend: ḍawʾ — “light”. At the end of a word after a sukūn the hamza sits on the line with no seat at all.
Read شَيْء right to left: sheen + fatha (sha), yaa with sukūn (y), hamza alone on the line (ʾ), then blend: shayʾ — “a thing”. Same seatless hamza as ضَوْء. Very common — you will meet it constantly.

Read قَرَأَ right to left: qaaf + fatha (qa), ra + fatha (ra), hamza on alif + fatha (ʾa), then blend: qaraʾa — “he read”. Lesson 1.12 promised this word would come back — here is the hamza it was hiding.

drills.title: ع or ء? — read down each column
drills.instructions: Each pair differs by one letter only. ع is squeezed in the middle of the throat and voiced; ء is a clean catch at the top. Read the pair back to back until they sound different.

audio.cue: Read عَمَل right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), meem + fatha (ma), lam (l), then blend: ʿamal — “deed, work”. ʿayn: squeeze the MIDDLE of the throat and voice it.
Read أَمَل right to left: hamza + fatha (a), meem + fatha (ma), lam (l), then blend: amal — “hope”. hamza: a clean catch at the very TOP of the throat. Nothing squeezes.
Read عَلَم right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), lam + fatha (la), meem (m), then blend: ʿalam — “flag, sign”.
Read أَلَم right to left: hamza + fatha (a), lam + fatha (la), meem (m), then blend: alam — “pain”.
Read عَرْض right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ra with sukūn (r), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: ʿarḍ — “width”.
Read أَرْض right to left: hamza + fatha (a), ra with sukūn (r), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: arḍ — “earth, land”. Both words end in ض — the FIRST letter is the only difference.

drills.title: ع inside real words — start, middle, end
drills.instructions: Read right to left. The ع gets harder as it moves toward the end of the word — the last row has nothing after the ع to lean on.

audio.cue: Read عَبْد right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ba with sukūn (b), dal (d), then blend: ʿabd — “servant”. The sukūn on ب gives you time to hold the ع open first.
Read عَسَل right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), seen + fatha (sa), lam (l), then blend: ʿasal — “honey”.
Read عَيْن right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), yaa with sukūn (y), nun (n), then blend: ʿayn — “eye; spring”. This is the letter’s own name — if you can say the word, you can say the letter.

Read عِلْم right to left: ʿayn + kasra (ʿi), lam with sukūn (l), meem (m), then blend: ʿilm — “knowledge”. ʿayn with a kasra is the hardest start of all — the throat wants to relax into a plain hamza.
Read عَصْر right to left: ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), ṣaad with sukūn (ṣ, heavy), ra (r), then blend: ʿaṣr — “afternoon, time”. Two back sounds in a row. The ص darkens the fatha before it.
Read بَعْد right to left: ba + fatha (ba), ʿayn with sukūn (ʿ), dal (d), then blend: baʿd — “after”. A sukūn’d ع mid-word gets squeezed — that squeeze is exactly the muscle to train.
Read بَعْض right to left: ba + fatha (ba), ʿayn with sukūn (ʿ), ḍaad (ḍ, heavy), then blend: baʿḍ — “some”.
Read جَعَلَ right to left: jeem + fatha (ja), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), lam + fatha (la), then blend: jaʿala — “he made”. Keep the ع voiced right through the middle — do not let it become a silent stop.
Read نَعَمْ right to left: nun + fatha (na), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), meem with sukūn (m), then blend: naʿam — “yes”. A word you can actually use out loud today.
Read مَعَ right to left: meem + fatha (ma), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), then blend: maʿa — “with”. Two letters — the easiest ع in the language. Start here if the others fight you.

Read سَمِعَ right to left: seen + fatha (sa), meem + kasra (mi), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), then blend: samiʿa — “he heard”. The vowel after the ع gives you somewhere to land — the easiest of the final group.
Read رَفَعَ right to left: ra + fatha (ra), fa + fatha (fa), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), then blend: rafaʿa — “he raised”.
Read رَجَعَ right to left: ra + fatha (ra), jeem + fatha (ja), ʿayn + fatha (ʿa), then blend: rajaʿa — “he returned”.

Read سَمْع right to left: seen + fatha (sa), meem with sukūn (m), ʿayn with sukūn (ʿ), then blend: samʿ — “hearing”. A bare ع at the very end with nothing after it — the hardest shape there is. Sustain it for a beat; do not drop it.
Read دَمْع right to left: dal + fatha (da), meem with sukūn (m), ʿayn with sukūn (ʿ), then blend: damʿ — “tears”. Same shape as سَمْع. Drill the two as a rhyming pair.

drills.title: ح inside real words
drills.instructions: Read right to left. Keep a hand on your throat: ح should feel tight in the middle, with no voice buzzing.

audio.cue: Read حَمْد right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), meem with sukūn (m), dal (d), then blend: ḥamd — “praise”. You hear this every day in al-Fātiḥah — anchor the ح sound here first.
Read حَقّ right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), qaaf with a shadda (qq — held double), then blend: ḥaqq — “truth”. Two throat sounds back to back. Keep ق deep and ح breathy; they are not the same place.
Read حَبْل right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), ba with sukūn (b), lam (l), then blend: ḥabl — “rope”.
Read حَجَر right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), jeem + fatha (ja), ra (r), then blend: ḥajar — “stone”.
Read حُبّ right to left: ḥaa + damma (ḥu), ba with a shadda (bb — held double), then blend: ḥubb — “love”. The damma rounds your lips — do not let the ح slide into a plain English ‘h’.
Read بَحْر right to left: ba + fatha (ba), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), ra (r), then blend: baḥr — “sea”. A sukūn’d ح is pure friction with no vowel to hide behind.
Read لَحْم right to left: lam + fatha (la), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), meem (m), then blend: laḥm — “meat”. Squeezed between two easy letters — listen for the ح vanishing entirely.
Read تَحْتَ right to left: ta + fatha (ta), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), ta + fatha (ta), then blend: taḥta — “under”.
Read سِحْر right to left: seen + kasra (si), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), ra (r), then blend: siḥr — “magic”. A sharp front hiss, then a deep throat breath — a big jump, made fast.
Read صُبْح right to left: ṣaad + damma (ṣu, heavy), ba with sukūn (b), ḥaa (ḥ), then blend: ṣubḥ — “morning”. A final ح is the one most often dropped. Finish the breath so it is audible.

drills.title: ح or خ or ه? — read down each column
drills.instructions: Each pair differs by one letter only. These are real, different words — the sound change changes the meaning.

audio.cue: Read حَلَقَ right to left: ḥaa + fatha (ḥa), lam + fatha (la), qaaf + fatha (qa), then blend: ḥalaqa — “he shaved”. The most consequential pair in the Qurʾān: get the ح wrong here and ‘He created’ becomes ‘he shaved’.

Read خَلَقَ right to left: khaa + fatha (kha), lam + fatha (la), qaaf + fatha (qa), then blend: khalaqa — “he created”. خ scrapes at the back of the mouth; ح is a clean breath lower down in the throat.
Read نَحْل right to left: nun + fatha (na), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), lam (l), then blend: naḥl — “bees”.
Read نَخْل right to left: nun + fatha (na), khaa with sukūn (kh), lam (l), then blend: nakhl — “date palms”.
Read فَحْم right to left: fa + fatha (fa), ḥaa with sukūn (ḥ), meem (m), then blend: faḥm — “charcoal”.

Read فَهْم right to left: fa + fatha (fa), haa with sukūn (h), meem (m), then blend: fahm — “understanding”. ه is a soft breath from the very top of the throat; ح squeezes in the middle. Hand on the throat: ح is tight, ه is loose.

drills.title: Hear a reciter say it — real Qurʾanic words
drills.instructions: These are the exact words as they appear in the Qurʾān, tanwīn and all. Tap each one to hear a qāriʾ say it, then copy him out loud.

dailyChecklist: Sukūn ladder read aloud once, every second letter stopped dead
Bounce-or-hold drill (مَطْ / مَظْ / مَدْ / مَذْ), 3 times through
Ten hamza words read aloud, naming the seat of each
ع word set — all three rows, with the final-ع row doubled
ح word set, then the ح/خ/ه pairs read across
Seven reciter words tapped and copied aloud

script: Open by naming the shift honestly: up to now she has been reading letters, and from today she is reading words. That is the whole point of Unit 1.4 — she recognises about 80% of letters on sight, and what remains is production inside real words.
Teach sukūn before hamza. Sukūn is purely mechanical and gives a quick win; hamza needs more talking.
Model the sukūn error before the correct form: say ‘baʿ-uh’ deliberately, ask her whether that sounds like one beat or two, then say ‘baʿ’. Naming the error first makes it audible when she does it.

Diagnostic for a stray vowel: have her say the unit while you clap on the stop. If her stop cannot land on your clap, there is a vowel hiding in there. A phone recording played back at half speed exposes it instantly and costs nothing at home.

GATE the qalqalah section. Run it only if her plain بَعْ / بَحْ stops are already clean. ‘Add a little bounce’ is heard by a beginner as permission to add a vowel — which is the exact error sukūn exists to prevent. If she is still saying ‘baʿ-uh’, skip qalqalah entirely today and say you will come back to it. A wrong qalqalah is worse than none.
Keep qalqalah minimal — قطب جد, a dry echo, that is all. If she asks how strong the bounce is, say it depends on position and that Phase 3 covers it. Do not open that door now.

Sequencing note for you, not for her: the standard Noorani order puts sukūn six chapters after harakat, behind tanwīn and madd. This course pulls it forward deliberately, because you cannot read a single real word without it — بَعْد, عِلْم, شَمْس are all unreadable with harakat alone. The risk that ordering guards against is teaching sukūn alongside harakat; here the harakat grid is already finished and drilled, so that condition does not apply.
For hamza, start from her own speech: have her say ‘uh-oh’ and then ‘apple apple apple’ slowly, and point out the catch she is already making. Then show that Arabic writes it down.

The seats are recognition-only today. She does NOT need to predict which seat a word takes — that is a Phase 2/3 spelling rule. Say so explicitly, or she will try to memorise a rule that has not been taught.
Pay off Lesson 1.12's promise out loud: قَرَأَ appeared there with a note that the hamza would be explained later. Show her the same word again now.

For ع vs ء run it in two stages. First RECEPTIVE only: you say one of the pair, she points at which it was — six trials, no speaking. Only then production, with her finger on her own throat. The finger does the diagnosis, which hands the check to her instead of keeping it in your ear.
رَأْس is the keystone item of the whole lesson — a sukūn sitting on a hamza. Close the throat, hold it, release straight into the seen. If she can do رَأْس, both halves of today have landed.
Do the ع and ح minimal pairs ACROSS, never down the column. Reading down lets her set the sound once and coast; reading across forces a switch on every item.
Close with the reciter clips. This is the first lesson in the course with real qāriʾ audio on tap — let her hear a fluent voice say the exact words she has just decoded.
listenFor: An extra vowel escaping after a sukūn (‘baʿ-uh’ for بَعْ) — the commonest sukūn error, and it turns one syllable into two.
A sukūn stretched into a long vowel. It is the opposite of a vowel; if it lengthens, the madd rules of Phase 3 will land on top of an error that is already fossilised.
ظ bounced like ط. ظ is NOT a qalqalah letter — if it bounces, she has substituted a heavy د. This is the single most useful contrast in the lesson.
ء substituted for ع (عَمَل read as أَمَل), the classic Phase 1 error already flagged in the Lesson 1.5 watchlist. Both words are real, so the mistake is invisible unless you are listening for it.
ع dropped entirely at the end of a word — سَمْع read as ‘sam’, دَمْع as ‘dam’. Nothing follows the ع to prop it up, so it simply disappears.
ح collapsing into ه once it is inside a word, even when the letter was solid in isolation. Test with بَحْر and صُبْح, not with حَمْد — حَمْد is often right by imitation alone.
ح hardening into خ under effort, especially when she is concentrating on something else in the word.
The seat being pronounced: ‘mu-w-min’ for مُؤْمِن, or a ‘y’ audible in بِئْر. The seat is silent furniture.
teacherNotes.homework: In the notebook: the sukūn ladder read aloud once daily, stopping every second letter dead. Bounce-or-hold drill (مَطْ / مَظْ / مَدْ / مَذْ) 3× through. The ten hamza words written out with the seat of each one named beside it. The ع word set daily — all three rows, with the final-ع row (سَمْع, دَمْع) read twice as often. The ح word set daily, then the ح/خ/ه pairs read across rather than down. Tap through the seven reciter words once a day and copy the qāriʾ aloud. Watch the 2-minute sukūn video once this week.
